title: What Is Phishing and How to Avoid It: A Practical Defense Guide
excerpt: Phishing is the leading cause of data breaches worldwide. Learn how to spot fake emails, websites, and text messages before they steal your credentials or money.
content:
What Phishing Is and Why It Works

Phishing is when attackers impersonate a trusted entity — your bank, Amazon, Google, your boss — to trick you into handing over credentials, payment details, or access. The name comes from 'fishing': casting a lure and waiting for victims to bite.

It works because it targets humans, not technology. You can have the strongest password in the world (use our password generator to make one), but if you're tricked into typing it into a fake login page, that password is now in the attacker's hands. Security technology can't save you from being fooled — which is why understanding the tactics is essential.

The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center consistently ranks phishing as the most reported cybercrime. In 2024 alone, reported losses from phishing-enabled fraud exceeded $3.5 billion in the US.

The Main Types of Phishing Attacks

  • Email phishing. Mass emails impersonating banks, streaming services, package delivery companies, or tech companies. These are sent to millions of people and rely on volume to find victims.
  • Spear phishing. Targeted attacks using information about you specifically — your name, employer, recent purchases. Much harder to spot because they feel personal and relevant.
  • Smishing (SMS phishing). Texts claiming to be from UPS, USPS, your bank, or a toll authority. The 'your package is held, click here' texts are a classic example.
  • Vishing (voice phishing). Phone calls from someone impersonating IRS agents, tech support, or bank fraud departments. They create urgency and ask you to provide codes or transfer money.
  • Clone phishing. A real email you actually received is copied and sent again with malicious links substituted. The attacker may already have access to an email account in your organization.

How to Identify a Phishing Attempt

Check these things before clicking any link or entering any credentials:

  1. Look at the sender's actual email address. Display names can say anything. Click the sender's name to reveal the real address. security@paypa1.com is not PayPal. support@amazon-helpdesk.net is not Amazon.
  2. Check the URL before clicking. Hover over links to see where they actually go. Phishers use tricks like: extra subdomains (paypal.com.badsite.com), homoglyph characters (pаypal.com with a Cyrillic 'a'), and hyphenated domains (paypal-secure-login.com).
  3. Look for urgency and threats. 'Your account will be suspended in 24 hours.' 'Unusual sign-in detected — confirm now or lose access.' Legitimate companies don't operate this way.
  4. Unexpected attachments. If you weren't expecting a document, invoice, or voicemail notification, don't open it. PDF and Word documents can contain macros that install malware.
  5. Requests for sensitive information. No legitimate bank, tech company, or government agency will ask for your password, full social security number, or credit card numbers via email or phone.

Real Examples to Learn From

The Amazon order confirmation scam: An email saying 'Your order has shipped — click here to track' goes to a fake Amazon login page that steals your credentials. The tell: you hover the link and see it goes to amazon-tracking-update.info, not amazon.com.

The Microsoft security alert: An email warning about 'suspicious activity on your Microsoft account' with a link to 'review recent activity.' The link leads to a convincing Microsoft login clone. The tell: the sender is microsoft-support@outlook-security.net, not @microsoft.com.

The CEO fraud / BEC attack: An email appearing to be from your company's CEO asking you to urgently wire money or buy gift cards. These are spear phishing attacks and are responsible for billions in annual losses. Always verify unusual financial requests via a phone call to the known number.

What to Do If You Clicked a Phishing Link

  1. Don't panic — just clicking a link usually isn't catastrophic.
  2. If you entered credentials: change your password immediately on the real site, then change it everywhere you used the same password (this is another reason not to reuse passwords).
  3. If you entered payment information: contact your bank or card issuer immediately to dispute charges and potentially freeze or replace the card.
  4. If you opened an attachment: disconnect from the internet and run a full antivirus scan. On Windows, use Windows Defender or Malwarebytes Free.
  5. Enable 2FA on the compromised account — even if the attacker got your password, 2FA will prevent them from logging in.

Tools That Help Protect You

Use a password manager — NordPass and 1Password both check URLs when they autofill, so they refuse to autofill credentials on phishing sites that don't match the real domain. This is a powerful automatic protection. See more recommendations on our recommended tools page.

Also consider a hardware security key (YubiKey) for high-value accounts. Hardware keys verify the exact domain during login, making them immune to phishing — they simply won't authenticate on a fake site.
